title: Holy, holy, holy (Apocalypse 4)
hook: around the throne the living creatures never stop singing

segments.voice: Yesterday, a lantern at an overgrown door. Your line was I stand and knock.

A door again, but this time it opens the other way. John writes: "behold a door was opened in heaven." A voice like a trumpet says, come up here. Suddenly John isn't looking at seven small churches in Asia anymore. Until now the book has kept its eyes on earth; here the camera swings up, through a doorway into the center of everything. And what John sees first isn't a battle, or a beast, or a timeline. It's worship.
screen: `A DOOR OPENED IN HEAVEN.` → `COME UP HITHER.` → `THE CENTER OF EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: John reaches for words. The one on the throne looks like jasper and sardine stone. A rainbow like emerald circles the throne. Lightning, thunder, seven burning lamps, and before it a sea of glass like crystal. Around it sit twenty-four elders in white, with gold crowns. Close around the throne, four living creatures: one like a lion, one like a calf, one with a man's face, one like a flying eagle, each with six wings and covered with eyes. Then the sound, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they rested not day and night, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come." Rested not: the song never stops. John's readers would have heard an echo. Long before, in the temple, the prophet Isaiah saw the seraphim crying to each other: "Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory." Holy is often explained as set apart, other, nothing like us; saying it three times piles it as high as the words will go. Then the elders fall down and cast their crowns before the throne. Every honor they have, they give back. Catholics know this song. At every Mass, at the end of the Preface, the priest speaks of joining the angels and saints in their hymn, and the people sing the Sanctus: holy, holy, holy. The Church says the Mass on earth joins the worship John saw through that open door. Later Christian tradition made the four creatures symbols of the four Gospel writers: Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the calf, John the eagle.
screen: `JASPER, EMERALD, A SEA OF GLASS.` · `FOUR LIVING CREATURES.` · `ISAIAH HEARD IT TOO.` · `THE SANCTUS AT EVERY MASS.` · then, large: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY, LORD GOD ALMIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Picture what John saw: the open door, the rainbow, the sea of glass, the creatures with their wings, the elders laying down their crowns, and let it be bright and loud. Then imagine the song has been going on the whole time, through every ordinary minute of your day. If you pray, join it softly, holy, holy, holy, once on each out-breath; if not, just listen in your mind to a song that never rests.
Holy. Set apart, wholly other. Sung three times by the creatures around the throne, and by the people at every Mass. Today's word.
Your line: they rest not. The song was going before you arrived. That's day six hundred twenty-four.

screen: `DAY 624 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LAMB THAT WAS SLAIN.`

original.note: Greek: holy, holy, holy (Apocalypse 4:8), echoing Isaiah's Hebrew qadosh.

trapdoor: what you thought: holy means very good, or very religious.
what it means: set apart, wholly other; the song of heaven, which the Church joins at every Mass in the Sanctus.
what a scholar hears: Apocalypse 4 reworks Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1; the Mass's Sanctus combines Isaiah 6:3 with the Hosanna of Matthew 21:9.
recall: the island where John saw the vision

chat.says: Why do we sing holy, holy, holy at Mass? Where does it come from?
options: From Isaiah's seraphim and the creatures around God's throne in the Apocalypse.
A medieval monk wrote it to give the choir a song before Communion.
It comes from the angels' song to the shepherds at Jesus's birth.
chat.meaning: In Apocalypse 4 the creatures cry holy, holy, holy day and night, echoing Isaiah's seraphim. The Sanctus at Mass joins that same worship.

seraphim.meaning: the angels Isaiah saw crying holy in the temple

Sanctus.meaning: Latin: holy; the hymn sung at Mass after the Preface

jasper.meaning: a precious stone John uses to describe the throne

Preface.meaning: the prayer at Mass that leads into the Sanctus

Isaiah.meaning: an Old Testament prophet who saw God in the temple

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the Sanctus comes at the end of the Preface, inside the Eucharistic Prayer, not 'just before' it (fixed); 'sardius' restored to the Douay 'sardine stone'; removed the etymology, 'strongest way', 'three chapters', 'centuries' and 'most common' claims; swapped the etymology myth for one from the text.
Hook: chapters 1–3 (the vision on Patmos and the seven letters) are earthbound; chapter 4 opens heaven. Confirm phrasing.
Throne description (4:3–7) paraphrased; 'sardine stone' in Douay-Rheims rendered as 'red sardius stone'.
Assignment of the four creatures to the evangelists follows Jerome (Irenaeus assigns them differently). Consider noting 'in the most common Western tradition'.
'Saying it three times is the strongest way the language knows' — Hebrew repetition for emphasis; confirm the phrasing.
Sanctus: Isaiah 6:3 plus Benedictus and Hosanna (Matthew 21:9). Current English text not quoted.
